docs.text: swjtumover ¶ Software for the swjtumover robot: it drives the wheels, reads the LiDAR, follows the black line, navigates a map, and runs the line-then-home mission. It runs on ROS 2 (the newer version of the robot framework this robot used before) and can be operated in two ways: what it means On the robot you open a terminal on the robot and type ROS 2 commands From your computer you use caasi , a tool that deploys the software to the robot, starts tasks there, and shows you their output from wherever you are There is no wrong choice. caasi adds records and remote control; the plain ROS 2 commands are exactly equivalent and always available. New to this? ¶ Read in this order: Getting started — prepare the robot, install caasi, connect the two, and run the robot for the first time. Start here if you have never set this up. Concepts — the handful of words you need: node, topic, service, launch, target, run. Skim it if you know ROS 2 already. Commands — every task, in both forms, with an example and a way to check it. Developing — write your own node or task, and run it on the robot. Troubleshooting — what to do when something does not behave. Before driving the robot, read Hardware and safety . What is in the package ¶ part contents swjtumover_msgs the message the motor driver publishes: currents, rpm, position, fault flags swjtumover_bringup motor driver, screen driver, launch files, configuration, task scripts swjtumover_vanjee LiDAR adapter, publishes /scan experiments/ one file per task, used by caasi to run it docs/ this manual (the pages you are reading) The robot ¶ item value body 0.32 × 0.30 m, 0.089 m tall LiDAR Vanjee 718H, single line, mounted at the centre of the body, 0.141 m up, tilted 1.5° wheels radius 0.05035 m, 0.206 m apart motor board 192.168.100.100 , UDP port 23 small display 192.168.100.100 , UDP port 26 internal networks LiDAR 192.168.110.x , motors 192.168.100.x Three things worth knowing before you start ¶ The LiDAR sits at the centre of the body. A distance it reports is measured to the centre; the front of the robot is 0.16 m closer to whatever it is measuring. The software accounts for this. The LiDAR must start first. The robot's programs compete for one network port (UDP 7000) and the LiDAR has to win it. The bringup does that in the right order for you. The motor driver stops by itself. If commands stop arriving, or the board stops answering, the wheels are driven to zero within half a second and the driver refuses to move until restarted.

docs.text: caasi in depth ¶ This chapter follows the way you actually use caasi: first contact with a robot, getting the code onto it, starting a task, watching it, and what to do when it misbehaves. Each command is shown with its arguments and a real example, so you can adapt rather than memorise. It covers what this robot needs; caasi is a general tool with more to it. Its home is https://github.com/7a6172/caasi/ , and every command answers --help with its own details. First contact ¶ You have the robot's address and an account on it. Register it once: caasi node enroll swjtumover05 --host 10.212.19.94 --user swjtumover argument meaning swjtumover05 the name you will use afterwards. It is the target's identity --host where the robot answers today ; it may change later --user the account caasi logs in as --port SSH port, default 22 --expect-fingerprint require a specific host-key fingerprint, if you were given one out of band On that first contact caasi records the robot's SSH host keys and some hardware facts. From then on it refuses a machine whose keys do not match — so a different robot at a recycled address cannot impersonate yours. Confirm what it recorded, and that the address still points at the same machine: caasi node identity swjtumover05 name: swjtumover05 machine_id: 2c7c442a1da846c6b70f5a2d7712d7db (from /etc/machine-id) cpu_model: Intel(R) N150 endpoint: 10.212.19.94:22, verified If the robot moved to a new address, do not re-enrol — follow it: caasi node refresh swjtumover05 Then see whether the machine is ready for this project at all: caasi node check swjtumover05 # reachable, environment sane caasi node inspect swjtumover05 # what hardware and software it has caasi target deps swjtumover05 --for bringup --for picks the part of the project you are asking about ( bringup , build , project , sim ). The last command prints a table of the requirements declared in caasi.yaml and whether each one is present on the robot : 17 installed, 0 missing, 0 incompatible, 0 optional-absent, 0 unknown Anything missing names the package to install. Getting the code onto the robot ¶ caasi deploy swjtumover05 The first deploy copies the whole project to ~/caasi/robots/swjtumover ; later ones send only what changed, which is why it is cheap to run after every edit. option when you want it --status show what is currently deployed, without deploying --dry-run preview what would be transferred --dest <path> deploy somewhere else, once --force deploy despite compatibility warnings from the preflight --list the deployment records caasi keeps for this project Then compile it there: caasi build --target swjtumover05 option when you want it -p <package> build one package, e.g. -p swjtumover_bringup --clean discard build/ , install/ and log/ first -j <n> limit parallel workers on a small machine --continue-on-error build the rest even if one package fails A build is recorded, so a run can tell you which build it used. Starting a task ¶ Every task is one file in experiments/ . You do not need to remember commands; you point at a file: caasi run start experiments/bringup.yaml -t swjtumover05 argument meaning experiments/bringup.yaml which task -t, --target which robot --name give the run your own name instead of the experiment's --dry-run print the command it would run, and start nothing --json machine-readable output, for scripting It answers with the run's name, which is what you use from then on: Run 20261029-023042-swjtumover-bringup started in background on target 'swjtumover05'. Follow it with: caasi logs 20261029-023042-swjtumover-bringup -f experiments/ covers bringup, mapping, navigation, the mission, the line follower, the obstacle guard, teleoperation, the camera, rviz, and starting/stopping the mission. Commands maps each task to its file. Watching it ¶ caasi logs 20261029-023042-swjtumover-bringup -f -f follows until the task ends; Ctrl+C stops following, not the task . Filters that save time: option use -n 50 only the last 50 lines, instead of following --stream stderr just what went to stderr --errors only lines that look like errors --component <name> only lines tagged with one component Anywhere a run name is expected you can also use a shorter form: a unique prefix, or latest : caasi logs latest -n 20 caasi run status latest For the state rather than the output: caasi run status 20261029-023042-swjtumover-bringup which reports whether it is running, stopped or failed, and which build and deployment it used — the fastest way to answer "is the robot running the code I think it is". caasi run attach <run> joins the live output and detaches with Ctrl+C without stopping anything. caasi run list shows recent runs; caasi run list -n 5 -t swjtumover05 narrows to one robot. When something is wrong ¶ Stop the task: caasi run stop 20261029-023042-swjtumover-bringup caasi run stop latest caasi run restart <run> starts the same command again as a fresh run, which is quicker than retyping the experiment path. If several things are running and you want the robot quiet: caasi run list # what is running caasi node occupancy # what caasi sees running on each target caasi run artifacts <run> lists files a task produced, and caasi run delete <run> forgets a finished run without touching the robot. Looking at the robot without a session ¶ Two commands cover it. caasi ros2 answers questions about the robot's ROS 2 system , and caasi exec runs anything else there. caasi ros2 list topics # every topic the robot publishes caasi ros2 list nodes # every node running on it caasi ros2 topic /scan # one topic: type, publishers, subscribers caasi ros2 node /motor_node # one node and what it is connected to caasi ros2 graph # the whole picture, as text caasi ros2 status # distro, install path, RMW, topic count caasi ros2 service list # services available on the robot caasi ros2 service call /line_then_home/start std_srvs/srv/Trigger "{}" caasi ros2 doctor # ROS 2's own health check, run there Every one of them takes --target, -t <name> , and omits it when you have run caasi choose target <name> . They run on the robot, so no local ROS 2 installation, no ROS_DOMAIN_ID matching and no DDS across the network is involved. caasi ros is the same command under its older name; both spellings work. For a single message rather than a summary, ask for exactly one: caasi ros2 topic /motor_state/left --echo --once caasi ros2 topic /cmd_vel --echo --once An unbounded stream is a run , not a query, so caasi stops short of one here. For a rate, or for anything else the ROS 2 tools do: caasi exec --ros -- ros2 topic hz /scan caasi exec --ros -- ros2 bag record -o /tmp/run1 /scan /odom caasi exec --ros -- bash -c 'ros2 param list /motor_node' option meaning --target, -t which robot; unnecessary once chosen --ros source the robot's ROS 2 setup first --overlay <path> also source this project's workspace, when a command needs the project's own packages --cwd <path> run the command in a given directory --env KEY=VALUE, -e set an environment variable, repeatable --timeout <seconds> give up after this long (default 60) --detach, -d run in the background as a managed run; pair with --name --ros matters for a reason worth knowing: a non-interactive SSH session does not read ~/.bashrc , so ros2 is not on the path unless caasi puts it there. That is why caasi exec -- ros2 … can fail while caasi exec --ros -- ros2 … works, and why caasi ros2 … needs no such care. Tools you will reach for eventually ¶ command what it tells you caasi doctor whether the robotics environment here is in order caasi info caasi's version, Python, and the toolchains it can see caasi system operating system, CPU, memory, processes caasi monitor CPU, memory and GPU while something runs caasi sensor which sensors and SDKs are visible caasi vision the computer-vision stack, e.g. whether OpenCV is usable caasi audit an account of the project and its reproducibility caasi check whether this project can run on this machine caasi view rviz open rviz for a run caasi view foxglove the same data in Foxglove Studio caasi teleop drive a robot, record demonstrations, replay bags caasi replay replay a recorded run without re-running it caasi ros2 list , caasi ros2 graph the ROS 2 graph, on this machine or on a chosen robot caasi ros2 runs where you point it: with no target it queries the machine you are sitting at, and with -t (or a chosen target) it queries the robot. A whole session, end to end ¶ The remote form, with the machine and robot chosen so neither is repeated: caasi choose target swjtumover05 # from here on, "the robot" caasi choose robot swjtumover # and the software on it cd <project> caasi node check swjtumover05 # is the robot there caasi target deps swjtumover05 --for bringup # does it have what we need caasi deploy # copy the code caasi build # compile it there caasi run start experiments/bringup.yaml # start the drivers caasi logs -f # watch until satisfied caasi ros2 topic /odom # is odometry arriving caasi exec --ros -- ros2 topic hz /odom # and at what rate caasi run stop latest # stop it The local form is the same page with the target set to local , or with caasi exec -t local for the one-off checks; the robot's own terminal needs none of it. What lives where ¶ what where the project on the robot ~/caasi/robots/swjtumover its deployment record ~/caasi/robots/swjtumover/.caasi-deployment.json per-run output on the robot <project>/.caasi/runs/<run>/stdout.log , stderr.log , exit_code your record of each run ~/.caasi/runs/<run>/ registered targets, and the chosen one ~/.config/caasi/config.yaml known host keys ~/.caasi/identity/

docs.text: Commands ¶ Every task, in the two places you might run it from: Local — on the robot itself. Both a plain ROS 2 command and a caasi run are given; they do the same thing, caasi adds a record. Remote — from another machine, through caasi. This is the normal way to operate a deployed robot. <target> is the execution target you enrolled in caasi — swjtumover05 for the robot. Run caasi choose target <target> once and you can leave -t off everywhere; every command below works either way. Each section also names the ROS 1 command it replaces, for comparison. 1. Bringup ¶ Starts the LiDAR adapter, both state publishers, the motor driver and the screen driver. Local # ROS 2 ros2 launch swjtumover_bringup bringup.launch.py # ROS 2 with rviz, or with the camera, or with a keyboard ros2 launch swjtumover_bringup bringup.launch.py enable_visualization:=true ros2 launch swjtumover_bringup bringup.launch.py enable_realsense:=true enable_teleop:=true # caasi, on the robot caasi run start experiments/bringup.yaml Remote caasi run start experiments/bringup.yaml -t <target> caasi logs 20261029-023042-swjtumover-bringup -f # follow the output caasi run status 20261029-023042-swjtumover-bringup caasi run stop 20261029-023042-swjtumover-bringup Check it worked ros2 topic hz /scan # ~14 Hz ros2 topic hz /odom # ~50 Hz ros2 topic echo /motor_state/left --once # fault flags false, rpm ~0 at rest ROS 1: roslaunch swjtumover_bringup bringup.launch 2. Teleoperation ¶ Arrow keys drive and turn: 0.2 m/s and 0.4 rad/s, accelerating at 0.2 / 0.4 per second. Local # ROS 2 (a terminal on the robot's desktop) scripts/run_teleop.sh # caasi, on the robot caasi run start experiments/teleop.yaml Remote Teleoperation needs the robot's display, so it is normally started as a run and driven while you watch the screen through a remote desktop session (see Remote access ): caasi run start experiments/teleop.yaml -t <target> caasi logs 20261022-101500-swjtumover-teleop -f Check it worked ros2 topic echo /cmd_vel # linear.x reaches ±0.2 while a key is held, 0 when released On a Wayland desktop the keyboard is only received while an X11 window has focus — click the rviz window first. Without any display the node exits with code 3 and says why. ROS 1: rosrun swjtumover_bringup teleop_node.py 3. Visualization ¶ Local # ROS 2 rviz2 -d "$(ros2 pkg prefix swjtumover_bringup)/share/swjtumover_bringup/config/bringup.rviz" # caasi, on the robot caasi run start experiments/rviz.yaml Remote # start rviz with the bringup in one go caasi run start experiments/bringup_rviz.yaml -t <target> # or rviz against a bringup that is already running caasi run start experiments/rviz.yaml -t <target> caasi logs <the rviz run> -f Check it worked: the robot body, /scan and the camera image draw with only the bringup running. The /map panel fills once something publishes a map; the two costmap panels need nav2 and are off by default. ROS 1: rosrun rviz rviz -d $(rospack find swjtumover_bringup)/config/bringup.rviz 4. Mapping ¶ Local # ROS 2 ros2 launch swjtumover_bringup slam.launch.py # caasi, on the robot caasi run start experiments/slam.yaml Remote caasi run start experiments/slam.yaml -t <target> caasi logs <the slam run> -f Check it worked ros2 lifecycle get /slam_toolbox # active ros2 topic hz /map # ~0.3 Hz once the robot moves ros2 run tf2_ros tf2_echo map odom # the transform exists ROS 1: roslaunch swjtumover_bringup bringup_gmapping.launch 5. Saving a map ¶ The target directory must exist; the service does not create it. Local mkdir -p ~/maps ros2 service call /slam_toolbox/save_map slam_toolbox/srv/SaveMap \ "{name: {data: '/home/swjtumover/maps/map'}}" Remote caasi exec --target <target> -- bash -c 'mkdir -p ~/maps && source /opt/ros/jazzy/setup.bash && \ ros2 service call /slam_toolbox/save_map slam_toolbox/srv/SaveMap \ "{name: {data: \"/home/swjtumover/maps/map\"}}"' | tail -2 nav2_map_server 's map_saver_cli does not work against slam_toolbox. ROS 1: rosrun map_server map_saver -f ~/maps/map 6. Navigation ¶ Local # ROS 2 -- serves the map, localises, plans and drives ros2 launch swjtumover_bringup navigation.launch.py # standalone test: let nav2 drive /cmd_vel directly ros2 launch swjtumover_bringup navigation.launch.py cmd_vel_topic:=/cmd_vel # caasi, on the robot caasi run start experiments/navigation.yaml Remote caasi run start experiments/navigation.yaml -t <target> Give it a pose — nav2 waits for one before activating its costmaps (the equivalent of rviz's "2D Pose Estimate"): ros2 topic pub --once /initialpose geometry_msgs/msg/PoseWithCovarianceStamped \ "{header: {frame_id: map}, pose: {pose: {position: {x: 2.85, y: -2.77, z: 0.0}, orientation: {w: 1.0}}}}" Send a goal ros2 action send_goal /navigate_to_pose nav2_msgs/action/NavigateToPose \ "{pose: {header: {frame_id: map}, pose: {position: {x: 2.0, y: -2.0, z: 0.0}, orientation: {w: 1.0}}}}" \ --feedback Check it worked for n in map_server amcl planner_server controller_server behavior_server bt_navigator velocity_smoother; do printf '%-18s ' "$n"; ros2 lifecycle get "/$n" done Navigation publishes /cmd_vel/nav ; the mission node owns /cmd_vel . ROS 1: roslaunch swjtumover_bringup map_server.launch , amcl.launch , move_base.launch 7. Line-then-home mission ¶ One launch brings up the bringup, all of nav2, the line follower and the mission — 21 nodes. docs.text: Concepts ¶ Short definitions of everything the rest of the manual assumes. Skip what you already know. ROS 2 in ten lines ¶ ROS 2 is the framework the robot's programs are built on. Programs are nodes ; they talk to each other over named channels. word meaning node one program doing one job, e.g. motor_node talks to the motor board topic a named stream of messages, e.g. /scan carries LiDAR readings 14 times a second message the data on a topic: a LiDAR scan, an odometry pose, a velocity command service a request/response call, e.g. "start the mission" and its answer action a long-running request with progress, e.g. "navigate to this point" launch file a script that starts several nodes with the right settings parameter a named setting a node reads at start-up, e.g. wheel radius TF the tree of coordinate frames; it lets a LiDAR reading be placed in the map lifecycle a node that must be activated before it works (navigation and mapping nodes) bag a recording of topics, so you can replay exactly what happened Commands you will use: ros2 node list # what is running ros2 topic list # what channels exist ros2 topic hz /scan # how often a topic publishes ros2 topic echo /odom --once # print one message ros2 service call <name> <type> "{}" # call a service ros2 launch swjtumover_bringup bringup.launch.py Coming from ROS 1, the names simply gained ros2 : ROS 1 ROS 2 roslaunch pkg file.launch ros2 launch pkg file.launch.py rosrun pkg node ros2 run pkg node rostopic / rosservice / rosnode / rosbag ros2 topic / ros2 service / ros2 node / ros2 bag rosparam parameters are per node: ros2 param get parameter server no global server; settings live with each node tf_echo (from tf ) tf2_echo (from tf2_ros ) caasi in ten lines ¶ caasi is the tool that puts the software on a robot and runs it from your computer. word meaning project this repository. caasi reads caasi.yaml to learn what it needs target a machine caasi can reach: the robot, or a workstation. You create one with caasi node enroll deployment a copy of the project on the target, under ~/caasi/robots/<project> build running colcon build on the target, recorded so runs know which build they used run one task started through caasi, with a name, a log, and an exit code exec a one-off command on the target, for quick checks scope ( --for bringup ) which part of the project you are asking about when checking dependencies A run is the thing you watch: caasi run status <run> , caasi logs <run> -f , caasi run stop <run> . Which robot am I talking to? ¶ Three different things are easy to confuse, because one machine carries two of their names. question answer example Which machine? the target — a registered user@host caasi can reach, or local swjtumover05 Which robot? the robot — the shipped software that drives its hardware swjtumover Whose work? the project — your own algorithm, task or homework, which uses that robot maze_run_1 caasi keeps the two apart on every machine it manages, so temporary work cannot damage the robot's own code: ~/caasi/ ├── robots/<robot>/ the shipped robot: its code and deployed environment. You do not edit this ├── projects/<project>/ your own work: algorithms, tasks, homework. It uses the robot's topics ├── workspaces/<name>/ a source checkout ├── data/ run logs, datasets, recordings, results └── artifacts/ cache/ build outputs, and scratch space that is safe to clear So swjtumover (robot) is the program that talks to motors, LiDAR and camera; maze_run_1 (project) is your code that subscribes to /scan and publishes to /cmd_vel . Same robot, your files in your own directory. Three machines, one tool ¶ The same distinction applies to where things run. A laptop may have no GPU and no robot attached: role what runs there caasi target your dev machine editing, small tests, nothing physical local (reserved name) the robot the hardware: motors, sensors, navigation swjtumover05 a GPU server Isaac Sim / Isaac Lab simulation, training e.g. gpu-01 All three are just targets to caasi; the difference is what you run on them. A robot has no GPU, so simulation goes to a GPU target — which may be your own machine if it has one, or a server elsewhere. Simulation and the GPU ¶ caasi sim , caasi lab and caasi train run Isaac Sim / Isaac Lab, which needs a real GPU. They take --target like everything else: caasi lab run experiments/warehouse.yaml -t gpu-01 caasi lab train experiments/warehouse.yaml -t gpu-01 caasi sim run experiments/scene.yaml -t gpu-01 and, more usually, you name the GPU machine once: caasi choose target gpu-01 --role gpu # everything sim/lab/train now goes there caasi choose # the "gpu work" row shows where that is A role never follows the machine you happen to be on. docs.text: Developing ¶ The tasks this robot ships with were written the same way you will write your own: a small Python node, a launch or experiment entry that runs it, and a caasi command that starts it here or on the robot. This chapter walks through that whole path once, with a complete program. Nothing here needs ROS 1 experience. Each ROS 2 idea is explained where it first appears. How a task is put together ¶ Three pieces, in three places: piece where what it is the node src/swjtumover_bringup/scripts/ the Python program that does the work the entry experiments/<name>.yaml how caasi starts it, with a name and a log the settings config/*.yaml , or a launch file in launch/ anything you want to change without editing code The existing tasks are exactly this: scripts/line_then_home.py is the mission, and experiments/mission.yaml is how it is started. Your first node ¶ This one only listens : it watches /odom , adds up the distance travelled, and prints it once a second. It never commands the motors, so you can run it while the robot is standing still, or on your own computer with no robot at all. Create the file src/swjtumover_bringup/scripts/distance_report.py : #!/usr/bin/env python3 """Report how far the robot has travelled, from odometry alone. Subscribes to /odom and prints the running distance once a second. Read-only: it publishes nothing, so it cannot move the robot. """ import math import rclpy from nav_msgs.msg import Odometry from rclpy.node import Node class DistanceReport(Node): def __init__(self) -> None: super().__init__("distance_report") # One setting, read when the node starts: seconds_to_run. self.declare_parameter("seconds_to_run", 10.0) self.seconds_to_run = float(self.get_parameter("seconds_to_run").value) self.total = 0.0 self.last = None self.elapsed = 0.0 # subscribe() says: call self.on_odom every time a message arrives on /odom. self.create_subscription(Odometry, "/odom", self.on_odom, 10) # A timer that fires every second, to print and to decide when to stop. self.create_timer(1.0, self.report) self.get_logger().info(f"reporting for {self.seconds_to_run:.0f} s") def on_odom(self, msg: Odometry) -> None: pose = msg.pose.pose.position here = (pose.x, pose.y) if self.last is not None: # Straight-line distance between two consecutive positions. self.total += math.hypot(here[0] - self.last[0], here[1] - self.last[1]) self.last = here def report(self) -> None: self.elapsed += 1.0 self.get_logger().info(f"travelled {self.total:.2f} m") if self.elapsed >= self.seconds_to_run: self.get_logger().info("done") raise SystemExit(0) def main() -> int: rclpy.init() node = DistanceReport() try: rclpy.spin(node) # keep running until the node is stopped except SystemExit: pass finally: node.destroy_node() rclpy.shutdown() return 0 if __name__ == "__main__": raise SystemExit(main()) What each part is, in ROS 2 terms: line meaning class DistanceReport(Node) a node : one program doing one job create_subscription(Odometry, "/odom", …) receive every message published on /odom declare_parameter("seconds_to_run", 10.0) a parameter : a setting an operator can override at start-up create_timer(1.0, self.report) call report once a second rclpy.spin(node) hand control to ROS 2 until something stops the node Comments and log strings are in English throughout this project — the ROS 1 code was in Chinese, and the ROS 2 side is kept in one language so logs can be read by anyone on the team. Make it runnable ¶ Two steps, both in the package. 1. Tell the build to install it. Open src/swjtumover_bringup/CMakeLists.txt and add your file to the existing install(PROGRAMS …) list: install(PROGRAMS scripts/teleop_node.py scripts/obstacle_rplidar.py scripts/omove_following_feng.py scripts/line_then_home.py scripts/distance_report.py # your new node DESTINATION lib/${PROJECT_NAME}) 2. Build. Locally: cd <project> colcon build --symlink-install --packages-select swjtumover_bringup source install/setup.bash On the robot, through caasi: caasi deploy # copies the new file caasi build # rebuilds there Run it locally (on your own computer) ¶ With the workspace sourced ( source install/setup.bash ), the ordinary ROS 2 way: ros2 run swjtumover_bringup distance_report.py ros2 run swjtumover_bringup distance_report.py --ros-args -p seconds_to_run:=3.0 argument meaning --ros-args -p name:=value set a parameter for this run only <node> --ros-args -r /odom:=/odom_filtered remap a topic name Without a running robot there will be no /odom , so it prints travelled 0.00 m and stops after ten seconds. That is the right result: your node works, there is simply nothing to listen to. Run it remotely (on the robot) ¶ caasi starts it the same way it starts the shipped tasks, so it gets a name, a log and an exit code. Create experiments/distance_report.yaml : # Run with: caasi run start experiments/distance_report.yaml [-t <target>] name: swjtumover-distance-report backend: python script: ../scripts/caasi_launch.py args: - run - distance_report.py - --ros-args - -p - seconds_to_run:=20.0 description: Prints the distance travelled, from odometry, for 20 seconds. Read-only. field meaning name how the run is listed and stopped backend python runs the script with the project's ROS 2 environment script caasi_launch.py is the launcher every entry point uses; it sources ROS 2 first args run <executable> maps to ros2 run swjtumover_bringup <executable> Start it, watch it, stop it: caasi run start experiments/distance_report.yaml -t swjtumover05 caasi logs -f # the newest run; Ctrl+C only stops watching caasi run status latest # running / stopped / failed caasi run stop latest # actually stop it Anything that starts a node belongs in experiments/ . That is what makes it repeatable: the same command works locally ( -t local , or no target at all), the output is kept, and the exit code tells you whether it really worked. The ROS 1 workflow opened a terminal, typed a command, and lost all of that. Debugging while you develop ¶ question command is my node publishing? caasi ros2 list topics what does one message look like? caasi ros2 topic /odom --echo --once what is it connected to? caasi ros2 node /distance_report is my node even running? caasi ros2 list nodes what did it print? caasi logs <run> only the errors caasi logs <run> --errors how fast is a topic? caasi exec --ros -- ros2 topic hz /odom record it and replay later caasi exec --ros -- ros2 bag record -o /tmp/run1 /odom /scan Add -t swjtumover05 when no target is chosen. Two tools are worth knowing at this point: caasi run list # every run you have started, with its status caasi exec --ros -- ros2 bag info /tmp/run1 # what a recording contains The tasks that already exist ¶ Read them in this order; each adds one idea to the one before. file what it shows scripts/obstacle_rplidar.py subscribing to /scan , deciding, publishing to /cmd_vel scripts/teleop_node.py reading the keyboard, publishing velocity, stopping when a key is released scripts/omove_following_feng.py vision: finding a line in the camera image and steering to it scripts/line_then_home.py the whole mission: states, a service to start it, nav2 goals, timeouts src/motor_node.cpp the actuator path, with its watchdog: what happens when commands stop arriving The ROS 1 originals of the last two are kept beside them as *_ros1.py / config/*_ros1.yaml , so you can compare what changed. Topic names, parameters and behaviour were preserved deliberately; where ROS 2 needed something different, the difference is commented in the file. House rules ¶ Comments and log strings in English. The ROS 1 files stay as they were, as references. Publishing to /cmd_vel moves the robot. Only one program should publish there at a time — /cmd_vel/line and /cmd_vel/nav are the arbitrated paths the mission uses. Publish rates and timeouts, not hope. The motor node zeroes the wheels if commands stop arriving; do not disable that. Test on a stand first. Wheels off the ground answer most questions before the robot can damage anything. Anything you want to keep goes in an experiment file , so a colleague can run it with one command. When your node works, the next useful step is usually to look at Commands for how the shipped tasks are driven, and Troubleshooting for when the robot misbehaves.

docs.text: Remote access and multiple robots ¶ Two practical questions once more than one robot runs this software: how to tell them apart, and how to see a robot's screen without sitting in front of it. Naming and identity ¶ Give caasi a target per machine , and let the software name stay swjtumover on all of them: targets: swjtumover05: host: 10.212.19.94 user: swjtumover tags: [robot, swjtumover, jazzy] deployment_root: "~/caasi/robots/swjtumover" swjtumover10: host: 10.212.19.105 user: swjtumover tags: [robot, swjtumover, jazzy] deployment_root: "~/caasi/robots/swjtumover" A machine that runs simulation rather than a robot is a target too — the same commands reach it: targets: gpu-01: host: 10.212.19.50 user: dev tags: [gpu, workstation, isaac] # no deployment_root: a non-robot target uses ~/caasi/workspaces/gpu-01 caasi choose target gpu-01 # run the simulator there instead of on the robot caasi node inspect gpu-01 # GPU model, VRAM, Isaac Sim / Isaac Lab availability caasi choose target swjtumover05 # back to the hardware Why this shape: the tag says what it is — swjtumover identifies the robot family, so every machine running this software is found with one query regardless of its number; the target name says which machine — used for addressing, nothing else; deployment_root keeps the on-robot path constant — every robot deploys to ~/caasi/robots/swjtumover , so documentation, scripts and muscle memory are identical everywhere. caasi does not rely on the name to recognise a machine. Enrolment records the machine itself: machine_id = 2c7c442a1da846c6b70f5a2d7712d7db (/etc/machine-id, strong) cpu_model = Intel(R) N150 ssh keys: ecdsa / rsa / ed25519 with SHA256 fingerprints endpoint: 10.212.19.94:22, verified A renamed robot or a changed address is still the same robot, because acceptance requires a matching enrolled host key. A different machine answering on a reused address is refused. The same physical box can carry two targets when it dual-boots (one per operating system); they are distinguished by machine id, which is exactly what that field is for. Working on one of several robots ¶ Every command takes -t <target> . Fix the one you are working on and stop repeating it: caasi choose target swjtumover05 # from now on, "the robot" caasi choose target swjtumover10 # later, another one caasi choose # which one is active, and where that came from caasi choose prints the machine it is about to act on, so switching between robots is visible rather than remembered. eval "$(caasi choose --session target swjtumover10)" switches for one terminal only — handy when two robots are on the bench at once. Keeping two robots' topics apart ¶ ROS 2 has no built-in isolation: two robots on one network, both on domain 0, see each other's topics. Give each its own domain when you provision it: caasi exec -t swjtumover05 -- \ bash ~/caasi/robots/swjtumover/scripts/provision.sh --apply --domain 5 This writes export ROS_DOMAIN_ID=5 into the robot's ~/.bashrc with the same guards as the ROS 2 lines, so every terminal on that robot uses its own domain. It also lets caasi rviz2 attach without being told the domain explicitly: an unknown domain is refused rather than assumed, because an assumed domain silently shows an empty graph. Seeing the robot's screen remotely ¶ The robot runs GNOME on Wayland, so classic VNC servers do not apply — they can only capture X11 windows, not the desktop. GNOME's own remote desktop is already part of the system and streams only the regions that change, which keeps it usable on modest hardware. Enable it once, on the robot, as the desktop user: grdctl rdp set-credentials <user> <password> grdctl rdp disable-view-only # omit to stay read-only grdctl rdp enable grdctl status # expect Status: enabled, Port: 3389 Then reach it without exposing a port on the network, by tunnelling over the SSH access caasi already manages: ssh -N -L 3389:localhost:3389 <user>@<robot> and point a client at localhost:3389 : Remmina — remmina -c rdp://localhost:3389 FreeRDP — xfreerdp /v:localhost:3389 /u:<user> Install one of them on the machine you sit at ( apt install remmina or freerdp3-x11 ). grdctl status is also the health check: if it reports a missing or invalid certificate, re-running grdctl rdp enable regenerates one. rviz on your own machine instead ¶ For data rather than a desktop, caasi can run rviz where you sit, against the robot's ROS 2 system: caasi choose target swjtumover05 caasi rviz2 caasi rviz2 --domain 5 # when --domain was given at provisioning time caasi resolves the target's distro, install path and domain, then runs the real rviz2 locally — it implements none of it. This depends on ROS 2 discovery reaching across the network between the two machines, which it does on one LAN and does not across two LANs joined only by a VPN such as Tailscale: there the graph appears empty even though the target was resolved correctly. That is a network fact rather than something caasi can arrange, and the RDP route above is the answer when you hit it. Notes ¶ The display is only needed for interactive work. Bringup, mapping, navigation and the mission all run headless, and that is the normal mode on a robot. Interactive extras need the desktop session's display. scripts/run_teleop.sh resolves it automatically (the X cookie on a Wayland session is a file whose name changes per session). If a viewer must run on a weak machine, prefer this RDP path over browser-based viewers: the encoding cost stays on the machine that owns the screen.

docs.text: Getting started ¶ From a robot that has never run this software and a computer that has never heard of caasi, to a robot doing something. Follow it in order the first time. Two machines are involved: the robot — Ubuntu 24.04, reachable over the network, your computer — where you type commands. Linux or macOS; Windows works through WSL. Nothing here assumes you have used caasi before, or ROS 2. Where a step has a local form (run on the robot itself) and a remote form (run from your computer), both are shown; you only need one. 1. Let your computer reach the robot ¶ On the robot, over a keyboard and screen or an existing session: sudo apt update && sudo apt install -y openssh-server sudo systemctl enable --now ssh command what it does apt install openssh-server installs the SSH server systemctl enable --now ssh starts it now, and again after every reboot Then, from your computer, confirm you can log in: ssh swjtumover@10.212.19.94 # your user and address Everything else can be done from your computer. You will not need the robot's keyboard again. 2. Install caasi on your computer ¶ pipx install caasi # recommended: keeps caasi in its own environment If pipx is not installed: sudo apt install pipx on Ubuntu, brew install pipx on macOS. Alternatives, if you prefer: pip install caasi # into the active Python environment python3 -m venv ~/.venvs/caasi && ~/.venvs/caasi/bin/pip install caasi # a dedicated environment Check it: caasi version caasi info # caasi, Python, and the toolchains it can see caasi lives at https://github.com/7a6172/caasi/ ; its README covers installation in more detail. 3. Register the robot with caasi ¶ A machine caasi may control is called a target . Register it once: caasi node enroll swjtumover05 --host 10.212.19.94 --user swjtumover argument meaning swjtumover05 the name you use from now on. It identifies the machine --host where the robot answers today; it may change later --user the account caasi logs in as On first contact caasi records the robot's SSH host keys and hardware identity, and later refuses to talk to a machine whose keys do not match that record. Name targets after the machine ( swjtumover05 , swjtumover06 , …). The software keeps the name swjtumover everywhere, so nothing you type afterwards depends on the robot's number. Verify it: caasi node list # your target appears caasi node identity swjtumover05 # enrolled keys and hardware, endpoint verified caasi node check swjtumover05 # reachable? environment sane? If the robot's address changes, tell caasi rather than re-enrolling: caasi node refresh swjtumover05 . 4. Put the code on the robot ¶ From the project directory — the one holding caasi.yaml : caasi deploy swjtumover05 It copies the project to ~/caasi/robots/swjtumover on the robot and verifies the copy. This needs nothing but SSH, so it works on a robot with no ROS 2 at all — which is exactly what step 5 then fixes. caasi deploy --status shows what is deployed and whether it verified. Re-run caasi deploy at any time; only what changed is transferred. 5. Prepare the robot once ¶ This is the step the ROS 1 setup scripts ( 1.ros_install.sh , 2.realsense_install.sh , 3.install.sh , 4.make.sh ) used to do by hand. It is now one caasi command, it is re-runnable, and it prints every command before running it. caasi run start experiments/provision.yaml -t swjtumover05 caasi logs -f # watch it work stage what it installs or changes ros ROS 2 Jazzy and colcon , if they are not already there packages the ROS 2 packages this project uses: navigation, mapping, camera, vision, teleop camera the video group for the camera, and a note about Intel's librealsense repository shell two guarded source lines in ~/.bashrc , so ros2 works in any new terminal build compiles the project Every stage is idempotent: running it a second time changes nothing. The shell lines it adds look like this, and are why ros2 topic list works in a fresh terminal afterwards: [ -f /opt/ros/jazzy/setup.bash ] && source /opt/ros/jazzy/setup.bash [ -f ~/caasi/robots/swjtumover/install/setup.bash ] && source ~/caasi/robots/swjtumover/install/setup.bash Several robots on one network. Give each its own ROS domain, so two robots do not see each other's topics: caasi exec -t swjtumover05 -- \ bash ~/caasi/robots/swjtumover/scripts/provision.sh --apply --domain 5 Local form. On the robot itself, the same script: cd ~/caasi/robots/swjtumover scripts/provision.sh # show what would be installed, change nothing scripts/provision.sh --apply # do it scripts/provision.sh --apply --stage ros # one stage only If the robot cannot reach the package servers, install ROS 2 by hand and skip the ros and packages stages — the list is in the ROS 2 chapter . 6. Check the robot has what the project needs ¶ caasi target deps swjtumover05 --for bringup It reads the requirements declared in caasi.yaml and checks each one on the robot : 17 installed, 0 missing, 0 incompatible, 0 optional-absent, 0 unknown --for selects the part of the project you are asking about ( bringup , build , project , sim ). Anything missing is named, with the package to install. 7. Build ¶ caasi build --target swjtumover05 This runs colcon build on the robot and records which build each run used. Step 5 already built it, so this is normally instant — run it again after you change code. 8. Run something ¶ caasi run start experiments/bringup.yaml -t swjtumover05 That starts the robot's drivers. It answers with a run name: Run 20261029-023042-swjtumover-bringup started in background on target 'swjtumover05'. Follow it with: caasi logs 20261029-023042-swjtumover-bringup -f Watch it, then stop it: caasi logs -f # the newest run; Ctrl+C only stops watching caasi run status 20261029-023042-swjtumover-bringup # running / stopped / failed caasi run stop 20261029-023042-swjtumover-bringup # actually stop it Ctrl+C while following logs does not stop the task. Use caasi run stop for that. Tired of typing -t ? ¶ Set the robot once, and the rest of the manual gets shorter: caasi choose target swjtumover05 caasi run start experiments/bringup.yaml # the same command, without -t caasi ros2 list topics # the robot's topics caasi choose with no arguments shows what is set and where each answer came from. See Concepts for what a project and a target are, and for --session , which scopes a choice to one terminal. The rest of this page uses the short form, assuming you set the target once. 9. Confirm it works ¶ caasi ros2 list topics caasi ros2 topic /scan The first lists what the robot publishes; the second prints one topic's type and how many nodes use it. You should see /scan , /odom , /motor_state/* and the rest. For rates and raw messages: caasi exec --ros -- ros2 topic hz /scan # about 14 per second caasi exec --ros -- ros2 topic echo /odom --once caasi exec --ros -- ros2 topic hz /odom # about 50 per second --ros makes caasi source the robot's ROS 2 setup for that one command, which is needed because a non-interactive SSH session does not read ~/.bashrc . Stop the bringup when you are done: caasi run stop latest 10. Where next ¶ Commands — drive it, map the space, navigate, run the mission. Each task has a local form, a remote form, and a way to check it. docs.text: Hardware and safety ¶ Read this before driving the robot. Interfaces ¶ what where motor / IO board 192.168.100.100 , TCP/UDP 23 (motors) and UDP 26 (display) Vanjee 718H LiDAR 192.168.110.100 , UDP 7000 on the host and 5000 on the LiDAR host addresses 192.168.100.10 (motor network), 192.168.110.10 (LiDAR network) The motor protocol is the board's own: 10-byte datagrams, CRC8-Maxim in the last byte, motor id 0x01 left / 0x02 right, speed as a signed RPM. Only the motor driver should talk to port 23. Safety model ¶ layer behaviour command watchdog motor.cmd_vel_timeout (0.5 s): no new /cmd_vel means zero speed feedback watchdog motor.motor_feedback_timeout (0.5 s): lost telemetry means zero speed, and the driver stays off until restarted fault latch any board fault flag (over-temperature, stall, phase overcurrent, overcurrent, sensor) latches the driver off body-aware guard the line follower holds zero when the centre clearance falls below 0.28 m navigation nav2's footprint critic rejects trajectories that would put the body into an obstacle A latched driver stays off deliberately: it means something real happened. Restart it after fixing the cause. Geometry ¶ The body is 0.32 × 0.30 m and the LiDAR is at its centre, so every range reading is measured to the centre while the body extends 0.16 m further forward. The line follower stops at 0.28 m of centre clearance (0.16 m body plus 0.12 m margin); nav2 uses the body footprint with footprint_padding: 0.06 . A single-line LiDAR sweeps one plane at 0.141 m. Objects shorter than that plane are not seen. Before driving ¶ Check the supply. The motor board goes quiet when the battery sags — it still answers ping while the protocol replies decay. If replies fall below roughly 95 %, charge it. Start the LiDAR first. Whichever process binds UDP 7000 keeps it; if the motor driver wins, there is no /scan . Never leave a publisher running. Every script here publishes a final zero and the watchdog covers the rest, but do not walk away from a live publisher. Set a pose before navigating. nav2 activates its global costmap only once map → base_link exists. Health checks ¶ ping -c3 192.168.100.100 # board reachable ros2 topic hz /scan # ~14 Hz ros2 topic hz /odom # ~50 Hz ros2 topic echo /motor_state/left --once # fault flags false, rpm ~0 at rest ros2 run tf2_ros tf2_echo base_link lidar_link # z = 0.14114 m, roll = 1.500° If something does not work ¶ symptom cause action no /scan another process holds UDP 7000 restart with the bringup, which orders it correctly no /odom , driver logs a feedback timeout then latches board silent: supply, cabling charge or repair, then restart the driver nav2 nodes stay inactive no map → base_link publish /initialpose map_server fails to configure map yaml path wrong image: in the yaml must be relative the robot does not move although /cmd_vel carries values driver latched, or the controller is publishing to /cmd_vel/nav restart the driver; check cmd_vel_topic keyboard teleoperation does nothing no X11 focus on a Wayland desktop click the rviz window, then use the arrow keys

docs.text: The body is 0.32 × 0.30 m and the LiDAR is at its centre, so every range reading is measured to the centre while the body extends 0.16 m further forward. The line follower stops at 0.28 m of centre clearance (0.16 m body plus 0.12 m margin); nav2 uses the body footprint with footprint_padding: 0.06 . A single-line LiDAR sweeps one plane at 0.141 m. Objects shorter than that plane are not seen.

docs.text: Check the supply. The motor board goes quiet when the battery sags — it still answers ping while the protocol replies decay. If replies fall below roughly 95 %, charge it. Start the LiDAR first. Whichever process binds UDP 7000 keeps it; if the motor driver wins, there is no /scan . Never leave a publisher running. Every script here publishes a final zero and the watchdog covers the rest, but do not walk away from a live publisher. Set a pose before navigating. nav2 activates its global costmap only once map → base_link exists.

docs.text: Troubleshooting ¶ Work down the list for the symptom you have. Every command that acts on the robot is given in the remote form; anything here also works locally, as in Commands . The robot does not move ¶ Check in this order — each step rules out the one below it. 1. Is anything even publishing a command? caasi ros2 topic /cmd_vel --echo --once -t swjtumover05 Nothing at all means no program is asking the robot to move — the mission is idle, or the controller is not running. If it prints linear: x: 0.0 , something is publishing but asking for standstill. 2. Is the motor driver still alive? caasi ros2 topic /motor_state/left --echo --once -t swjtumover05 If this prints nothing, the driver has stopped talking to the motor board. Its log says why: caasi logs latest --errors A line like this means the board went quiet — usually the battery: motor feedback timeout, locked to zero speed; left gap 21.4s, right gap 21.4s The driver latches off in that case and will not move until restarted: charge the robot, then caasi run stop <the bringup run> and start it again. 3. Is the driver refusing because of a fault? /motor_state/… carries five flags — over-temperature, stall, phase overcurrent, overcurrent, sensor. Any of them true is why. Restart after fixing the cause; the latch is deliberate. 4. Is navigation the one holding the robot back? If you are driving with nav2, remember it publishes /cmd_vel/nav , and the mission node is what sends that to /cmd_vel . For a standalone navigation test, launch it with cmd_vel_topic:=/cmd_vel . There is no LiDAR data ¶ caasi exec -t swjtumover05 --ros -- ros2 topic hz /scan Nothing, or the log says the adapter could not open a port: something else took UDP 7000 . The LiDAR has to start before the other programs, which bringup.launch.py does for you — if you started nodes by hand, stop everything and use the launch file. Navigation does nothing, nodes stay inactive ¶ caasi exec -t swjtumover05 --ros -- ros2 lifecycle get /amcl inactive means nav2 has not been told where the robot is. Give it a pose; the equivalent of clicking "2D Pose Estimate" in rviz: caasi exec -t swjtumover05 --ros -- ros2 topic pub --once /initialpose \ geometry_msgs/msg/PoseWithCovarianceStamped \ "{header: {frame_id: map}, pose: {pose: {position: {x: 0.0, y: 0.0, z: 0.0}, orientation: {w: 1.0}}}}" If a launch was already aborted by the time you set the pose, restart the navigation launch — a lifecycle manager that has given up does not retry. Bring nav2 up before the camera. With the camera streaming at full rate during start-up, the lifecycle transitions slow down badly on a small machine and the manager can give up. The mission will not start ¶ caasi run start experiments/mission_start.yaml -t swjtumover05 It prints the service's answer. The two common ones: answer meaning no /amcl_pose and no map -> base_link transform yet: set an initial pose first the robot does not know where it is — see the pose command above /line_then_home/start is not available -- is the mission launch running? experiments/mission.yaml is not running rviz shows nothing, or "frame [map] does not exist" ¶ map only exists once localisation or mapping is running. With just the bringup, the fixed frame odom is the right one — the shipped configuration already uses it, so a "map does not exist" error means an older configuration file is in use. If the robot model is missing while everything else draws, the description did not reach rviz; the shipped configuration asks for it correctly, so check you are loading config/bringup.rviz and not another file. The map panel stays empty until something publishes /map . The two costmap panels need nav2 and are off by default. Keyboard teleoperation does nothing ¶ The node needs a display. If it prints keyboard teleoperation: node started it is listening, and the likely reason keys do nothing is focus: on a Wayland desktop the keyboard is only received while an X11 window has focus, so click the rviz window first. If it exits with code 3 instead, there is no display at all — run it from a terminal inside the robot's desktop session, or through a remote desktop session (see Remote access ). caasi cannot reach the robot ¶ caasi node check swjtumover05 unreachable — the robot is off, or on a different address. caasi node refresh swjtumover05 re-verifies and follows it. identity mismatch — the machine answering is not the one you enrolled. Do not re-enrol blindly: confirm which robot it is, then caasi node reenroll if the hardware legitimately changed. slow or flaky — small machines over Wi-Fi drop connections. Retry; a run that reports lost started but its wrapper could not be placed. caasi run start again after the link settles. A run reports failed immediately ¶ caasi logs <run> --errors The usual causes: the service it needed was not running (see the mission above), the robot's build is older than the code you think it has ( caasi run status <run> names the build), or a package is missing ( caasi target deps swjtumover05 --for bringup ). Starting over cleanly ¶ caasi run list # stop anything running caasi run stop <each run> caasi build --target swjtumover05 --clean caasi deploy swjtumover05 caasi build --target swjtumover05 If you moved or renamed the project directory on the robot, a clean build is required: the build system records absolute paths and refuses to reuse them elsewhere.
